mastery.oneLine: Gentle, rhythmic rocking of a joint, graded I to IV by how far into the range you go, chosen by how irritable the patient's pain is.
mastery.whatItIs: Maitland mobilization is a hands-on method where you move a joint passively (the patient stays relaxed) in small, smooth, repeated oscillations. The 'grade' tells you how big the movement is and how deep into the joint's range you work. You use it to calm pain or to stretch a stiff joint, then immediately check whether the patient's own movement improved.
mastery.analogy: Think of pushing a child on a swing. Tiny, gentle pushes near the middle calm the swing; bigger pushes toward the end of the arc stretch it out. You choose the push size by how touchy the swing is today, not by what the swing is called.
coreIdeas: Treat the patient's movement problem, not a scan or a diagnosis name. Pick one movement or symptom (the 'comparable sign'), treat, then test it again.
Pain-dominant and easily flared joints get small, gentle Grades I-II. Stiff but comfortable joints get Grades III-IV that reach into the resistance.
Reassessment decides everything. If the comparable sign does not improve, change the glide, the grade or the whole plan. Never just push harder.

terms.meaning: The one movement or symptom you test before and after treatment, for example neck rotation to the right or shoulder lifting to 90 degrees.
A tiny joint glide the patient cannot do on their own, such as one vertebra gliding forward. You produce it with your hands.
How easily symptoms flare, how bad they get, and how long they take to settle. High irritability means be gentle.
P1 is where pain first starts as you move the joint. R1 is where you first feel resistance. These two points guide your grade.

I: small movement at the start of range. II: large movement in the free part of range. III: large movement into resistance. IV: small movement into resistance. Grade V is a thrust and is a different technique.

whenToUse: A painful, stiff joint where one movement clearly reproduces the patient's pain (positive comparable sign).
Pain-dominant, irritable joints (use Grades I-II) or stiffness-dominant, calmer joints (use Grades III-IV).
Stiffness after immobilisation or injury once the tissue is safe to load.
whenNot: Unstable fracture, dislocation, active infection, or suspected cancer in the area.
Worsening neurological signs, or uncertainty about blood vessel safety (especially in the neck).
Take extra care in hypermobile joints, recent trauma and highly irritable pain.

steps.title: Choose and record the comparable sign
steps.detail: Example: right neck rotation reaches 50 degrees and pain starts at 45. Write it down so you can prove change later.

steps.title: Screen for red flags
steps.detail: Ask about night pain, unexplained weight loss, recent trauma, dizziness or neurological symptoms before touching.

steps.title: Position for comfort
steps.detail: Support the joint so surrounding muscles can relax. A guarding muscle will block any glide you try.

steps.title: Place a broad, specific contact
steps.detail: One hand fixes the bone that should stay still. The other contacts the moving bone close to the joint line. Take up the skin slack first so you move the joint, not the skin.

steps.title: Use your body weight, not your fingers
steps.detail: Lean smoothly through relaxed arms. Finger-only pressure makes jerky, painful oscillations.

steps.title: Start low and ask
steps.detail: Begin with a low grade. Local pressure is fine. Sharp pain, pins and needles or symptoms spreading down the limb mean stop.

steps.title: Treat, rest, then retest
steps.detail: After a set, ask the patient to repeat the comparable sign. Keep, progress or change the technique based on that answer.

steps.title: Hand the gain back to the patient
steps.detail: Finish with active movement or loading in the new range, so the improvement is used rather than lost.

mastery.dose: Typical teaching range: about 1-2 oscillations per second, 30-60 seconds per set, 2-4 sets. Grades I-II for pain, III-IV for stiffness. This is a starting point; the patient's response sets the real dose.

example.patient: Ravi, 45, bank clerk, right-sided neck pain since a long drive four days ago.
example.assessment: Right rotation is 50 degrees with pain at the end. Pain eases within a minute of resting, so irritability is low. Screening is clear. A gentle press on the right C5 joint reproduces his pain.
example.treatment: In lying, Ravi relaxes while you apply a Grade III unilateral PA glide at C5 for 30 seconds, three sets, asking about symptoms after each set.
example.reassess: Rotation improves to 65 degrees with less pain. You teach him gentle active rotation every hour and review in two days. If rotation had not changed, you would try another level or direction instead of pressing harder.

mistakes: Picking a grade from the diagnosis name instead of irritability and response.
Moving the whole limb instead of producing a true, specific joint glide.
Feeling a joint 'loosen' under your hand but skipping the retest of the patient's own movement.

selfTest.q: A very irritable shoulder: which grades and why?
selfTest.a: Grades I-II. They are small and gentle and aim to calm pain without provoking a flare.

selfTest.q: The joint feels smoother but the patient's neck turn is unchanged. What have you proved?
selfTest.a: Only that your hand felt something. Trust the comparable sign, not your feel, and rethink the plan.

mastery.recap: Test the movement, choose the glide and grade, test the movement again.
mastery.evidence: Reviews support manual therapy, including mobilization, for short-term pain and function in several joint problems, usually alongside exercise. How it works is uncertain. It does not 'put a joint back in place', and one technique should not be promised to fix a specific structure.

depth.why: A passive oscillation moves the joint surfaces by accessory (arthrokinematic) glide. The immediate effect in most patients is better explained by mechanical and neurophysiological pain modulation (descending inhibition, changed stretch tolerance) than by a lasting change in joint position. Grades I-II work inside the range and target pain; grades III-IV reach the limit of the range and target stiffness; grade V is a small thrust at the end of range.
choose: Pain dominates and irritability is high: grades I-II, short bouts, reassess after each.
Stiffness dominates with low irritability: grades III-IV, longer bouts, the barrier is the target.
Choose Kaltenborn when the capsular pattern and convex-concave direction are the question; choose Mulligan when a painful active movement can be made pain-free with a glide.
A joint that is already hypermobile or unstable is not a target for stretching grades.
parameters: small amplitude at the start or through the range, about 1-2 oscillations per second, 30-60 s per bout
large amplitude to the limit (III) or small amplitude at the limit (IV), about 2 oscillations per second, 30-60 s per bout, 1-3 bouts
along the treatment plane, or the accessory glide that matches the restricted physiological movement
2-3 sessions a week early on, then fade as active movement returns
depth.progress: Regress by lowering the grade, shortening the bout or moving away from the barrier. Progress by moving from I-II to III-IV, then add active movement (the patient moves while you hold the glide) and loaded range.
measure: Pain at rest and at the target movement (0-10)
Active and passive range with the same goniometer position
A patient-specific functional task (for example reaching, turning to reverse park)
Joint-play quality and end-feel compared with the other side
depth.evidence: Reviews show small-to-moderate short-term gains in pain and range for many joints, with the effect larger when combined with exercise. The specific grade or direction is rarely proven superior, and long-term benefit beyond the session depends on active rehabilitation.
pitfalls: Treating the joint you can reach instead of the one the examination implicated.
Using a stretching grade in an irritable joint and flaring it.
Not re-testing the comparable sign after every bout, so the effect is assumed.
Stopping at the passive gain without converting it into active control.
screen: Suspected fracture, infection, tumour or inflammatory arthropathy in flare
Cauda equina or cord signs; vertebrobasilar insufficiency signs for the neck
Marked hypermobility or ligament instability at the segment

heading.en: The Maitland grades, one by one
heading.ur: Maitland ke grades, ek ek karke

intro.en: A grade is a pairing of how big the movement is and where in the range it happens. Pick the grade from pain, irritability and stiffness, then reassess.
intro.ur: Grade yeh batata hai ke movement kitni badi hai aur range ke kis hisse mein hoti hai. Grade dard, irritability aur stiffness dekh kar chunein, phir reassess karein.

tag.en: Small movement at the start of range
tag.ur: Range ke shuru mein chhoti movement

what.en: Small oscillations at the very start of the range. For pain and high irritability.
what.ur: Range ke bilkul shuru mein chhoti oscillations. Dard aur zyada irritability ke liye.

en: Position the joint in a comfortable resting position.
Oscillate gently, well before any resistance.
ur: Joint ko aaramdeh resting position mein rakhein.
Kisi bhi resistance se kafi pehle narmi se oscillate karein.

what.en: Large oscillations that stay inside the free range and do not reach resistance. For pain.
what.ur: Badi oscillations jo free range ke andar rehti hain aur resistance tak nahi pohanchtin. Dard ke liye.

ur: Poore waqt resistance se pehle rahein.

what.en: Large oscillations that go into the resistance and the tissue limit. For stiffness.
what.ur: Badi oscillations jo resistance aur tissue limit mein jati hain. Stiffness ke liye.

en: Take the movement firmly up to the limit.
Watch the patient's response and retest.
ur: Movement ko limit tak mazbooti se lein.
Patient ka response dekhein aur retest karein.

what.en: Small oscillations at the limit of the range. For stiffness where only the end range is tight.
what.ur: Range ki limit par chhoti oscillations. Us stiffness ke liye jahan sirf end range tight ho.

ur: Retest karein aur dard provoke na karein.

tag.en: Small, fast thrust at the end

what.en: A small, fast thrust at the end of range (manipulation). Needs specific training and screening.
what.ur: Range ke end par chhota, tez thrust (manipulation). Khaas training aur screening maangta hai.

en: Screen for red flags and obtain consent.
Deliver the small, fast movement as trained.
ur: Red flags screen karein aur consent lein.
Training ke mutabiq chhoti, tez movement dein.

watch.en: Only with formal training; do not use in an irritable joint.
watch.ur: Sirf formal training ke saath; irritable joint mein nahi.

urdu.short: Maitland Joint Mobilization mein therapist joint ko patient ki taraf se relax halat mein chhoti, narm aur rhythm ke sath aagay-peechay harkat deta hai. Harkat ka grade patient ke dard, sensitivity aur stiffness ke mutabiq chuna jata hai. Maqsad sirf joint ko move karna nahi, balkay dekhna hai ke patient ki asal takleef wali movement ya function mein behtari aati hai ya nahi.

details.heading: Yeh technique kya hai?
details.text: Maitland mobilization mein therapist joint ko patient ke relaxed rehne ke dauran passive taur par chhoti, smooth aur baar-baar dohrayi jane wali oscillations se move karta hai. Grade batata hai ke movement kitni bari hai aur joint ki range mein kitni door tak jati hai. Is ka maqsad dard ko kam karna ya stiff joint ko stretch karna ho sakta hai; is ke baad patient ki apni movement dobara check ki jati hai.

details.heading: Misal se samjhein — analogy ka tarjuma
details.text: Isay jhoolay ko dhakka dene jaisa samjhein. Darmiyani range mein chhotay aur narm dhakkay jhoolay ko calm karte hain; arc ke aakhir ke qareeb baray dhakkay usay zyada stretch karte hain. Dhakkay ka size aaj ki sensitivity ke mutabiq chuna jata hai, sirf technique ke naam se nahi.

details.heading: Bunyadi ideas
details.text: Patient ki movement problem ko target karein, scan ya diagnosis ke naam ko nahi. Ek movement ya symptom ko comparable sign ke taur par select karein, treatment se pehle note karein aur baad mein dobara test karein. Dard se jaldi bharrak uthne walay joint mein Grades I–II ki chhoti aur narm movements use ki ja sakti hain; zyada stiff magar relatively calm joint mein Grades III–IV resistance ki taraf jati hain. Agar comparable sign behtar na ho to glide, grade ya poora plan dobara dekhein—sirf zyada zor na lagayein.

details.heading: Aham istilahat
details.text: Comparable sign: woh movement ya symptom jo treatment se pehle aur baad test hota hai, jaise neck ko right ghumana ya shoulder uthana. Accessory movement: joint ki chhoti glide jo patient khud paida nahi kar sakta. Irritability: symptoms kitni asani se barhte hain, kitne shadeed hote hain aur settle hone mein kitna waqt lete hain. P1 dard shuru hone ka point hai; R1 resistance pehli baar mehsoos hone ka point hai. Grades I–IV movement ki amplitude aur range mein position batate hain; Grade V thrust hai aur alag technique hai.

details.heading: Kab use karein aur kab ehtiyat karein?
details.text: Yeh approach us waqt consider ki ja sakti hai jab joint painful ya stiff ho aur koi movement patient ki pehchani hui takleef ko reproduce kare. Stiffness after immobilisation ya injury mein bhi sirf tab consider karein jab tissue ko load dena safe ho. Unstable fracture, dislocation, active infection ya us area mein cancer ka shak ho to routine mobilization na karein. Barhtay neurological signs ya neck mein blood-vessel safety ke bare mein uncertainty ho to ruk kar munasib assessment karein. Hypermobility, recent trauma aur bohat irritable pain mein extra ehtiyat zaroori hai.

details.heading: Steps — source ka tarjuma
details.text: 1. Comparable sign choose aur record karein; misal ke taur par right neck rotation 50 degrees tak pohanchti hai aur 45 degrees par dard shuru hota hai. 2. Red flags screen karein, jaise raat ka dard, baghair wazeh wajah weight kam hona, recent trauma, chakkar ya neurological symptoms. 3. Joint ko comfortable position mein support karein taake aas-paas ke muscles relax kar saken. 4. Ek hand se us bone ko stabilize karein jo still rehni chahiye aur doosray se joint line ke qareeb moving bone par specific contact banayein; pehle skin ka slack lein. 5. Sirf fingers se zor dene ke bajaye relaxed arms aur body weight se smooth movement dein. 6. Low grade se shuru karein aur patient se symptoms poochhein. Tez dard, pins-and-needles ya limb mein phailti symptoms hon to rok dein. 7. Set ke baad comparable sign dobara test karein aur response ke mutabiq technique rakhein, badlein ya progress karein. 8. Aakhir mein active movement ya loading karwayein taake patient nayi range ko khud use kare.

details.heading: Dose — source mein di gayi teaching range
details.text: Aam teaching range takreeban 1–2 oscillations per second, har set 30–60 seconds aur 2–4 sets hai. Dard ke liye Grades I–II aur stiffness ke liye Grades III–IV ka zikr hota hai. Yeh sirf starting range hai; asal dose patient ke response ke mutabiq hoti hai.

details.heading: Clinical example — original source ka tarjuma
details.text: Ravi, 45 saal ka bank clerk, chaar din pehle lambi drive ke baad neck ke right side dard report karta hai. Right rotation 50 degrees hai aur end par dard hota hai; aaram karne se dard ek minute mein kam ho jata hai, screening clear hai aur right C5 joint par gentle pressure usi dard ko reproduce karta hai. Lita kar Ravi ko relax rehne diya jata hai aur C5 par Grade III unilateral PA glide 30 seconds ke liye, teen sets mein apply ki jati hai; har set ke baad symptoms poochay jate hain. Dobara test par rotation 65 degrees tak behtar hoti hai aur dard kam hota hai. Phir gentle active rotation har ghantay sikhayi jati hai aur do din baad review hota hai. Agar rotation na badalti to zyada zor lagane ke bajaye doosra level ya direction consider ki jati.

details.heading: Aam ghaltiyan
details.text: Diagnosis ke naam se grade chun lena, irritability aur response ko nazar-andaz karna; poori limb ko hila dena magar specific joint glide na dena; ya hand ke neeche joint smooth mehsoos hone par patient ki apni movement dobara test na karna.

details.heading: Self-test
details.text: Sawal: Bohat irritable shoulder mein kaun se grades aur kyun? Jawab: Grades I–II, kyun ke in ki movement chhoti aur narm hoti hai aur maqsad flare kiye baghair dard ko calm karna hota hai. Sawal: Joint smooth mehsoos ho magar patient ki neck rotation na badlay to kya prove hua? Jawab: Sirf yeh ke therapist ke hand ko kuch mehsoos hua; comparable sign ko follow karein aur plan dobara dekhein.

details.heading: Recap aur evidence — original source ka tarjuma
details.text: Movement test karein, glide aur grade chunein, phir movement dobara test karein. Reviews ke mutabiq manual therapy, mobilization samet, kai joint problems mein short-term pain aur function mein madad de sakti hai, aam tor par exercise ke sath. Is ka mechanism yaqini taur par maloom nahi. Yeh joint ko 'wapas jagah par bithana' nahi hai aur kisi ek technique se kisi specific structure ko theek karne ka wada nahi karna chahiye.

details.heading: Misal — sirf samjhane ke liye
details.text: Agar kisi ko shoulder upar uthate waqt dard ho, to therapist pehle range aur dard note kar sakta hai, phir assessment ke baad munasib gentle trial karke movement dobara check kare. Yeh fictional teaching example hai, kisi patient ke liye treatment recommendation ya guaranteed outcome nahi.

deeper.heading: Clinical reasoning
deeper.text: Maitland approach mein passive joint movement ko symptoms aur examination findings ke mutabiq select kiya jata hai. Pehle comparable sign, irritability, range aur patient ka goal samjhein. Har painful joint ko same grade ya same direction ki mobilization dena sahi nahi.

deeper.heading: Grades aur application ka concept
deeper.text: Oscillatory mobilization ke grades amplitude aur available range ke relation mein samjhe jate hain. Grade ka selection pain, stiffness, irritability aur treatment objective par depend karta hai. Exact joint handling aur force control supervised practical training se seekhein.

deeper.heading: Common mistakes aur reassessment
deeper.text: Baseline record kiye baghair treatment karna, har patient par ek hi grade repeat karna aur symptoms barhne ke bawajood continue karna avoid karein. Session ke baad wahi movement, pain aur function dobara assess karein.

deeper.heading: Evidence aur limits
deeper.text: Mobilization short-term pain ya movement mein kuch patients ko madad de sakti hai, magar response har condition mein same nahi. Isay guaranteed joint correction ya standalone cure ke taur par explain na karein.

cue.wake: A stiff joint is not a locked door. Please don't arrive carrying an imaginary hammer.
cue.question: If the joint feels smoother under your hand but the patient's original turn is unchanged, what have you proved?
cue.answer: Only that your hand felt something. Check the same movement and rethink the plan.
cue.easy: Comparable sign = the exact movement or symptom you test before and after.
cue.remember: Test the turn, choose the glide, test the turn again.

technique.storyHeadline: The movement stops. But what is really stopping it?

episode.patient: A driver comes in because checking the blind spot has become a little adventure—and not the fun kind. When they turn the head, a familiar ache appears before the movement is finished. You note the direction, the range and what happens afterward. That's your baseline, not a verdict about a 'stuck vertebra.'
episode.decision: After screening and gaining consent, you choose a comfortable position and a graded oscillatory input. The direction, grade and duration are selected to explore the symptom response—not to prove you can produce the strongest mobilization.
episode.retest: Now the driver turns to check that imaginary blind spot again. If it is easier, you may have created a useful window for active movement. If it is unchanged, you change the hypothesis rather than turning up the force.
episode.spark: Your thumbs are asking questions, not issuing traffic tickets.

aha.hook: The joint doesn't come with a 'stiffness meter.'
aha.analogy: Think of Maitland as a careful conversation: you ask a question with a graded oscillation, and the patient's movement replies. A harder question is not automatically a smarter one.
aha.challenge: After the mobilization, the joint feels softer under your hand—but neck rotation is unchanged. Is the technique a success?
aha.reveal: Not yet. Palpated feel alone is not the goal. Recheck the familiar movement, symptoms and function, and revise the plan if nothing meaningful improves.

weave.dialogue: Patient: 'Can you unlock this neck?' Clinician: 'First, let's see exactly which turn feels locked.' The hands do not get to start the story until the patient's movement has introduced the problem.
weave.watch: Picture the shoulders resting against the table, not creeping toward the ears. The contact is specific, the oscillation controlled, the patient's expression readable. The clinician stops briefly. 'Turn again—same speed, same direction.' Suddenly the reassessment feels like the plot twist, not a formality.
weave.method: A grading system is a useful vocabulary, not an automatic volume knob. A sore, irritable presentation may need a gentler trial; a stiffer but comfortable presentation raises different questions. Nobody wins extra marks for reaching a higher grade.
weave.science: Think of the nervous system as a mixing desk, not a jammed door hinge. Sensory input, expectation, motor guarding and tissue loading may all influence the final experience. One better head turn does not tell us which slider moved.
weave.question: The clinician thinks a segment feels 'looser', but the patient's original neck turn is unchanged. What should guide the decision?
weave.answer: The original comparable movement and symptom response. Record the finding, reconsider the technique or dosage, and avoid claiming a vertebra was mechanically realigned.
weave.closer: The thumb supplies the question. The patient's movement writes the answer.

patientPosition: Place the patient in a relaxed position where the target joint is fully supported and the painful muscles do not need to hold the limb.
Expose only the region you need. The patient should feel safe, warm and able to tell you immediately if symptoms change.
Start in the joint position that produces the least guarding. In a highly irritable patient, do not force the joint into end range before you begin.
therapistPosition: Stand close to the treatment table so your body weight, not only your hands, controls the movement.
Keep your shoulders relaxed, elbows soft and spine neutral. A stable therapist position makes the mobilization smoother and safer.
Position yourself in line with the intended accessory glide so the force travels through the joint in a clean direction.
handPlacement: One hand stabilizes the proximal bone or segment. The other hand contacts the moving bone as close to the joint line as is comfortable and anatomically safe.
Use a broad contact whenever possible. Avoid pressing directly on sensitive nerves, vessels, bony prominences or healing tissue.
Before mobilizing, gently take up skin slack so your hands move the joint rather than simply rubbing over the skin.
forceDirection: Apply the accessory glide in the direction selected from examination and the comparable sign.
Grades I and II use small-amplitude oscillation in the early to mid range when pain and irritability dominate.
Grades III and IV move further into resistance when stiffness is the main limitation and the joint is safe to mobilize.
The force should be rhythmic and controlled. It should never feel like a sudden uncontrolled push.
applicationSteps: 1. Record the comparable sign first: for example shoulder abduction pain at 90 degrees, knee flexion limit, or painful cervical rotation.
2. Screen red flags, instability, fracture risk and neurological concerns before treatment.
3. Position and stabilize the joint. Find the direction of accessory movement you want to test.
4. Begin with a low grade. Ask the patient what they feel: local pressure is acceptable; sharp pain, distal symptoms or neurological change is not.
5. If symptoms settle and the joint remains relaxed, continue the selected oscillation for the planned set.
6. Rest, then immediately repeat the original comparable sign.
7. If pain or movement clearly improves, you may repeat the technique or progress the grade. If nothing changes, change the direction, grade or treatment choice.
8. Finish by using the gained movement actively: active ROM, motor control, strengthening or a meaningful functional task.
expectedResponse: A useful response is less pain, easier movement, increased range, reduced guarding or improved function immediately after the set.
Temporary mild local soreness can occur, but the patient should not leave with a major flare or new distal symptoms.
stopCriteria: Stop if pain becomes sharp, severe or unfamiliar.
Stop if symptoms spread distally, numbness/weakness develops, dizziness occurs, or the patient feels unsafe.
Stop if repeated sets create progressively worse range or pain.
commonMistakes: Choosing a grade because of the diagnosis instead of irritability and response.
Moving the whole limb instead of producing a true accessory glide.
Using fingers alone and creating jerky oscillations.
Continuing because the joint 'feels stiff' even though the patient's comparable sign is worse.
Failing to reassess after the technique.
clinicalExample: Example: a patient with painful shoulder elevation has restricted posterior glide. Record active elevation, apply a comfortable posterior glide, then retest elevation. If elevation becomes easier, follow with active reaching and rotator-cuff loading so the manual gain becomes functional.

mechanism.mechanismMap: Rhythmic joint movement → mechanoreceptor input + altered nociceptive signaling → spinal/supraspinal pain modulation + reduced guarding → easier movement → active loading
mechanism.simpleExplanation: Maitland mobilization probably works through several systems at the same time. The oscillatory movement gives the nervous system repeated non-threatening mechanical input, can reduce pain sensitivity for a period, may reduce protective muscle guarding, and can temporarily improve how easily the joint moves. The important point is that the treatment does not simply 'push a joint back into place'.
stepByStep: 1. The therapist applies a controlled accessory movement to the joint.
2. Joint, capsule, skin and muscle mechanoreceptors detect the movement and pressure.
3. This sensory input reaches the spinal cord and brain and can compete with or modify nociceptive input.
4. Segmental spinal mechanisms and descending pain-control pathways may reduce pain sensitivity temporarily.
5. When pain and threat decrease, protective muscle activity can reduce and the patient may tolerate more movement.
6. Repeated loading can also produce small temporary changes in joint/capsular mechanics and stretch tolerance.
7. The new movement window is most useful when it is immediately reinforced with active movement and exercise.
physiology: Peripheral sensory effect: low-threshold mechanoreceptors in skin, capsule, muscle and periarticular tissue respond to pressure and movement.
Spinal effect: altered afferent input can influence dorsal-horn processing and reduce amplification of nociceptive signals.
Supraspinal effect: the brain can change pain perception through descending inhibitory/facilitatory pathways involving brainstem and cortical networks.
Neuromuscular effect: reduced threat and altered sensory input may lower protective co-contraction or muscle guarding.
Mechanical effect: joint surfaces and periarticular tissues are loaded, but evidence that long-lasting structural repositioning is the main mechanism is weak.
Contextual effect: expectation, trust, explanation, therapist contact and perceived safety can change pain and movement responses and are part of the total treatment effect.
clinicalTranslation: Grades I–II are often useful when pain/irritability is dominant because the goal is symptom modulation, not forcing range.
Grades III–IV are used more when stiffness is dominant, but the patient response still decides whether they are appropriate.
A useful sign is an immediate improvement in the comparable movement or task, not simply the therapist feeling more joint play.
myths: Do not claim that the technique permanently 'puts the joint back in place'.
Do not assume a click or large movement is required.
Do not assume one accessory glide mechanically corrects the exact structural cause of pain.
mechanism.evidenceNote: Current evidence supports a complex mix of peripheral, spinal, supraspinal, neurovascular and neuromuscular responses. The exact mechanism that produces the clinical benefit in an individual patient is still uncertain.

mechanismEvidence.summary: Manual therapy does not have one universal mechanism. Modern evidence supports interacting peripheral, spinal, supraspinal, neurovascular, neuromuscular and contextual responses. The exact mechanism responsible for a patient's clinical improvement is often uncertain.
mechanismEvidence.sourceTitle: The mechanisms of manual therapy: A living review of systematic, narrative, and scoping reviews

room.arrival: The patient turns toward the window. Their chin stops early; their shoulder rises to finish the turn. 'There—that's my usual pain.' You mark this exact movement before placing your hands.
room.touch: With the body supported, test an appropriate graded oscillation, monitoring symptom behavior and the person's comfort rather than trying to force a particular joint feel.
room.retest: Ask for the same window turn. A calmer movement supports continued active practice; no change means a different clinical question, not more force.
